summary: Documents Microsoft's extensions to the PPP Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol, usually called MS-CHAP, used to authenticate users on point-to-point links. It is informational and describes a vendor's protocol rather than an IETF standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2433 describes Microsoft's version of CHAP authentication over PPP. It defines how peers exchange a challenge and response, how failures can allow retries, and how an expired password can be changed.

how does ms-chap respond to a challenge
subtitle: Microsoft's PPP CHAP dialect for authenticating remote workstations.

tldr.problem: Microsoft wanted remote workstations using PPP to use authentication compatible with its Windows network environment.
tldr.mechanism: MS-CHAP negotiates a distinct CHAP algorithm value and defines response fields, failure reasons, retry behavior and password-change packets.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo documents the protocol, but its IESG note warns that MS-CHAP has significant vulnerabilities.

today: RFC 2433 is an Informational memo published in October 1998, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its IESG note warns that the protocol has significant vulnerabilities.

sections.title: Purpose and Negotiation
sections.content:
MS-CHAP is Microsoft's dialect of the PPP Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP). The memo says it was created to authenticate remote Windows workstations while providing functionality used on Windows networks. It follows standard CHAP where possible.

PPP negotiates MS-CHAP through the Link Control Protocol (LCP). Its configuration follows standard CHAP except that the Algorithm field uses 0x80 instead of the MD5 value 0x05. The Challenge packet has the standard CHAP format, and its challenge value is 8 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: MS-CHAP is Microsoft's variation of CHAP authentication for PPP. The peers select it during PPP setup using a different algorithm value from standard CHAP.

sections.title: Challenge Response and Success
sections.content:
The Response packet keeps the standard CHAP format but divides its Value field into a 24-octet LAN Manager response, a 24-octet Windows NT response and a 1-octet flag selecting the Windows NT response. The RFC says LAN Manager response use is deprecated and recommends that peers leave that field zero-filled and set the flag to use the Windows NT response.

The Name field identifies the account and may include a Windows NT domain. A Success packet uses the standard CHAP format. The memo describes the responses as encoded functions of the password and received challenge.
sections.plainLanguage: The response includes separate fields for LAN Manager and Windows NT challenge responses. The memo marks the LAN Manager response as deprecated and recommends selecting the Windows NT response.

sections.title: Failure Reasons and Retries
sections.content:
The Failure packet includes formatted text with an error code, a retry flag, an optional new challenge and a protocol version. The listed error codes include restricted logon hours, disabled account, expired password, no dial-in permission, authentication failure and a password-changing error.

If the retry flag is set, the authenticator disables short timeouts and expects the peer to prompt the user for new credentials and send another response. If no replacement challenge is included, the RFC defines how the next challenge is derived from the previous one. The version field helps select the password-change packet type.
sections.plainLanguage: A failure message can say why authentication failed and whether the user may try again. It can also provide a new challenge and identify the protocol version.

sections.title: Changing an Expired Password
sections.content:
The protocol defines two Change Password packet formats for changing the account password named in the preceding Response. A peer sends one only after the authenticator reports the password-expired error, code 648. Version 1 is deprecated and peers should not transmit it; version 2 is selected when the failure message reports version 2 or greater.

The version 1 packet has Code 5 and Length 72. The version 2 packet has Code 6 and Length 1118. Both use encrypted password-related fields, and the RFC describes version 2 support in certain Windows NT and Windows 95 versions at the time it was written.
sections.plainLanguage: An expired password can be changed after the server reports error 648. The RFC describes two packet formats and marks the older version 1 format as deprecated.

sections.title: Security Warning
sections.content:
The RFC's IESG note warns that the protocol has significant vulnerabilities. In its security section, the memo explains that the challenge is sent in clear text and is used with a password hash to form the response, allowing passive known-plaintext and active chosen-plaintext attacks against that hash.

The memo recommends limiting password retries and taking precautions such as frequent password changes where eavesdropping is likely. It states that the version 1 Change Password packet must not be sent when eavesdropping is possible because an observer can reveal the new password hash.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC warns that MS-CHAP has significant vulnerabilities. A listener can use captured challenges and responses to attack password hashes, so the memo recommends limiting retries and avoiding the version 1 password-change packet when eavesdropping is possible.
